name: Hang-Hi Quiet Apartments
subtitle: Second floor. Suspended from above. Nobody has ever explained from what.
description:
Home, insofar as the word survives contact with the building. The second floor hangs from something overhead rather than standing on anything below, and the residents treat this as a design feature the way other towns treat a nice cornice. Your corridor runs from the stair to your door in a length that has never twice been the same, and it is longer tonight, because you are walking it alone.

Inside, the flat has arranged itself into the shape it uses when you have been away: chair angled toward the window, desk under its usual weight of paper, the smell of wet wool coming off the coat you have not yet taken off. The lamp is on. You do not recall leaving it on, but the lamp and you have an arrangement and it has never yet been in writing.
revisit:
The corridor gives you a different length again — shorter this time, companionably so, which from this building reads less like an anomaly and more like a courtesy extended to a tenant who has had a long day.

The green flame in the wall lamp is doing what it does. Somewhere below, a bucket is set down on tile and a squeegee starts an arc. Two flats along, a door opens onto weather that is not the weather outside, and closes again, and nobody comes out.

Your own door is where you left it. Two-F. The window in it has been sorted, completely sorted, and you would not want to worry about the weather in it.

lucid.2: Under everything else, at the edge of the audible, there is a rhythm in the building that is not plumbing. Three or four strikes, then a pause. Then three or four more.
lucid.3: The pauses between the strikes have lengths. Some are short. One, tonight, goes on for most of a minute, and the building holds its breath through all of it, and then the striking resumes and something in the arrangement of your evening has been revised.
lucid.4: The building is not making a sound. The building is being described as making a sound, and the description is being typed, and you are standing inside the paragraph where it happens.

ambient: Somewhere below, a squeegee completes an arc, and for a moment the whole stairwell agrees to be a stairwell — the angles settle, the flight lands where the eye expects, the handrail runs true from top to bottom. It holds for about as long as the wet takes to dry.

A door two flats down opens onto weather. It is not the weather outside — it is warmer, and it is raining in it, and there is a smell of cut grass in a building four streets from the sea in the middle of a fog. Nobody mentions it. The door closes. The corridor smells of grass for a while afterwards.

The green flame in the corridor lamp throws four shadows across the wall and has only ever had the one of you to work with. They do not agree about where the light is. Three of them move when you move.

The lift goes down without being called, waits at the bottom for the length of a held breath, and comes back up empty. The doors do not open. It has done this twice tonight and the building has not remarked on it.
Somebody on the floor above crosses the room, stops in the middle, and stands there. There is no second set of footsteps and no conversation and no chair being sat in. After a while they cross back.

objects.name: the waterlogged notebook
objects.description:
It came out of the harbour in your coat pocket, and it came out heavy, and it has not got appreciably lighter since. Ninety pages of blue smear — ink gone entirely to weather, whole leaves fused into a single blue block at the fore-edge, the whole record of whatever you were doing before the sky handed you back reduced to a colour.

The binding held. That is worth noting on its own: cheap stitching, sea water, several hours, and the block has not come out of the case.

Three pages are dry.

Not dried, which would leave a tidemark and a cockle and a stiffness in the paper. *Dry*, as though they were never in the water — flat, supple, taking a fingernail the way dry paper does. They sit in the middle of the ruin like a paragraph the flood was instructed to go around, and there is smeared blue on the page before them and smeared blue on the page after.

The handwriting is yours. The words are yours in the specific sense that you would use those words, in that order, with that comma in that place. And you have no memory whatsoever of the sentence they make.
objects.repeat: The three pages are still dry. You have stopped expecting this to change and you have not stopped checking, and the checking has become a small private ritual performed at the start of every look, like a man testing a step he already knows will hold.
objects.monocle: Through the gold, the smeared pages stay smeared — but the blue moves. It is not ink dispersing in water. It is ink being *withdrawn*, page by page, back toward a nib, in a slow careful retraction that has been going on for some time and is nearly finished. The three dry pages are not survivors. They are what has not been taken back yet.

passive.text: Water does not select. It has no criteria and no opinions and no way of forming either. A flood that takes ninety pages and goes round three, in the middle of a bound notebook, in a coat, in the sea, is not a flood that failed to reach them. It is a flood that was routed around them.

Read the three pages as a person rather than as evidence. The hand is steady on the first, hurried on the second, and on the third it is doing something worse than hurried — it is *careful*, letter by letter, the way a man writes when he has decided this may be the only copy and somebody else is going to have to read it.

clue.title: Three dry pages
clue.text: The notebook drowned. Three pages in the middle did not, and they carry your handwriting and a sentence you have no memory of composing.

clue.title: The ink is being withdrawn
clue.text: Through the monocle, the ruined pages are not running. They are being un-written, slowly, back toward a nib.

check.prompt: There are more pages in this than the three. Ninety of them, and the blue has not left the paper, it has only stopped being arranged. Work the smear apart with a dry cloth and a great deal of patience and see what is still in there.
check.success:
Patience, a dry cloth and a very shallow angle. Two more pages come up out of the blue — not legible, but *ruled*, and the ruling is not the notebook's.

Somebody drew a margin down these pages by hand, twice, on the same two sheets, at eleven and nine inches. The measurements of a room.
check.failure: The blue is not ink any more, it is a suspension, and the moment the cloth touches it the page decides to be one colour all the way through.

clue.title: Margins at eleven and nine
clue.text: Two ruined notebook pages carry hand-drawn margins at eleven and nine inches — the measurements of a room.

objects.name: the hallway mirror
objects.description:
A tall spotted glass in a frame that the building insists came with the building, which is the sort of claim this building makes about everything in it and has never once been asked to support.

It reflects the corridor, the wall lamp, the coat rack, and you — in roughly that order of enthusiasm, as though you were the item it was least contractually obliged to include and is including out of politeness.

Hold still in front of it. Hold still for longer than is comfortable, longer than a man checking his collar would, long enough that the holding becomes a thing you are consciously doing rather than a pause.

On a long enough hold, the corridor behind your reflection stops being the corridor. It becomes a room with a low ceiling and one lamp with a green shade, and a desk under the lamp, and a great deal of paper on the desk, and a chair pushed back from it.

Then it is the corridor again. And the mirror has the decency not to look pleased with itself about any of it.
objects.repeat: The office comes faster now. Either you have got better at holding still or it has got worse at pretending, and there is no version of that sentence in which the situation is improving.

lucid.3: This time the office holds for four full seconds, and there is a hand in it. Not reaching for anything. Resting beside the paper, the way a hand rests when the person it belongs to is deciding.
lucid.4: The hand in the mirror is the same shape as yours and is not doing what yours is doing.

objects.monocle: The gold lens declines to reflect the corridor at all. It gives you the room directly, without the pretence: a desk, a lamp with a green shade, a typewriter with a page in it, and the page has a paragraph on it, and the paragraph is about a man standing in a hallway looking into a mirror.

passive.text: The trick is stillness. Not patience — stillness, which is a different discipline and a harder one. Whatever is on the other side is watching for movement the way anything watches for movement, and it is very good at it, and it has had considerably more practice at this than you have.

Rule out the ordinary, in order, and be honest at each step. Reflected room from a facing window: there is no facing window, this wall backs onto the stair. Trick of the frame: the frame is deal, forty years old, and came with the building. A second room beyond a partition: you have measured the corridor and the flat and there is nothing between them but eleven inches of lath.

That exhausts the ordinary. What is left is a room that is not in this building, arriving in a mirror that is.

check.prompt: Hold absolutely still. Longer than is reasonable, longer than is comfortable, long enough to be rude to your own knee — and do not look at the room, look at the place in the glass where the room stops agreeing with itself.
check.success:
You hold. Your knees file their complaint and you overrule it. The corridor drains out of the glass like water out of a bath and the office stays: a desk, a green lamp, a typewriter with a page in it, and beside the page, a coffee cup with a ring under it that has been there long enough to have a ring.

Somebody works here. Somebody has worked here for a long time, badly, in the specific way of a person who does not get up.
check.failure: Your knee goes at forty seconds — the one that has been going since the harbour — and the shift is small and the mirror is not interested in small. The corridor snaps back. The coat rack is very smug about it.

clue.title: The office behind the mirror
clue.text: A low room with a green-shaded lamp, a desk, a typewriter with a page in it, and a coffee ring old enough to be a habit.

clue.title: Something behind the glass
clue.text: There is a room behind the mirror that is not the corridor. Forty seconds of stillness is not enough to furnish it.

objects.name: the snake on the building sign
objects.description:
HANG-HI QUIET APARTMENT , says the board over the entry — the gap at the end sized for a letter that is not there, because the final S was supplied years ago by somebody with a spray can, a steady hand and a considerable sense of humour.

It is a snake. Coiled into the shape of the letter, green on a ground of flaking gold, tail tucked under to close the lower curve, head laid along the upper one.

It is a good S. It is a considerably better snake.

It has been in a different coil every single time you have had occasion to look at it, over eleven years, in every light and every weather — and you have never once caught it moving. Not a shimmer, not a settle, not the wrongness of a thing that has just stopped. After the first year you gave up trying, and after the second you decided to regard the whole arrangement as manners.
objects.repeat: Recoiled. Same paint, same flaking at the tail, same wall — and a different S, in a slightly different place, doing a slightly different amount of work to hold the name together.
objects.monocle: Through the gold, the snake is not paint and is not a snake. It is a correction — a letter that was typed wrong, struck through, and typed again, and the strike-through is what you have been reading as a body all these years. It is still wet. It has been still wet since before you moved in.

passive.text: A building that cannot hold on to the last letter of its own name. There is no reading of that which is about paint. A name is an argument a place makes about itself, and this one keeps losing the end of the sentence, and somebody keeps going up a ladder to put it back.

clue.title: A correction, still wet
clue.text: The snake that serves as the building's final S is, under the monocle, a strike-through: a letter typed wrong and typed again. The ink has not dried in eleven years.

check.prompt: The snake on the board is in a slightly different position every time the eye comes back to it. Look away deliberately, count to four, and come back fast enough to catch it mid-move.
check.success:
Away and back, fast, without deciding to.

It is mid-stroke. Not mid-slither — mid-*stroke*, the way a line is mid-stroke when a hand is drawing it, and there is no hand, and it finishes the stroke while you watch and settles into having always been that shape.
check.failure: Away and back. Coiled, painted, flaking at the tail, and exactly where it was, and it will go on being exactly where it was for as long as you keep doing this.

clue.title: Caught mid-stroke
clue.text: The snake on the Hang-Hi sign is caught mid-stroke — a line being drawn, finishing itself, with no hand drawing it.
clue.source: the snake on the building sign

objects.name: Landy's repair notices
objects.description:
Lying Landy, the Unhandy Dandy, does not fix things. Landy files.

Pinned to the corridor board in a fan of municipal beige is the complete record of his attentions to this building, and it is a substantial document. WINDOW 2F — WEATHER NONCONFORMING — RESOLVED. DOOR 2C — OPENS TO 3A ON THURSDAYS — RESOLVED. STAIR, THIRD FLIGHT — COUNT — RESOLVED. CORRIDOR — LENGTH — RESOLVED, RESOLVED, RESOLVED.

The window in 2F still has weather in it. The door in 2C still opens onto 3A on Thursdays, and the residents of both have arranged their Thursdays around it.

Each form is stamped, bottom right, with a four-lobed seal and a line of small print in a face slightly smaller than the rest: FILED WITH THE COALITION FOR CULPABILITY AND CONSTRUCTIVE CHANGE. NO FURTHER ACTION IS REQUIRED OF THE RESIDENT. NO FURTHER ACTION IS AVAILABLE TO THE RESIDENT.

The last two sentences are not the same sentence, and they have been printed together on every form in the fan.
objects.repeat: Three more since you last looked. The corridor has been RESOLVED twice this week, which is once more than it has been complained about, which means Landy is now filing against a schedule rather than against events.
objects.monocle: Under the gold, the word RESOLVED is not a word. It is the same three characters typed over and over on top of themselves until the paper gave up and agreed to be black there. Nothing was resolved. Something was insisted on, at length, by a machine.

passive.text: Nothing on this board has been repaired. Every item on it has been *filed*, and the distinction is the whole of Landy's professional life. A repair changes the building. A filing changes the record of the building. Only one of those has been happening here for eleven years.

Read the small print again, properly. 'No further action is required of the resident' is a courtesy on the face of it and an instruction underneath it, and the difference between those two readings is the difference between a landlord and something considerably more organised.

And it appears on every form. Twenty-two times. In the same words.

clue.title: The four-lobed seal
clue.text: Every impossibility in this building has been filed with the Coalition for Culpability and Constructive Change and marked RESOLVED. None of them has been fixed.

check.prompt: Twenty-two forms in a cupboard on a half-landing, all stamped, all in the same hand. You have read enough municipal paper in your life to know what a form is supposed to look like. Read these as documents rather than as excuses.
check.success:
A repair notice exists to create a liability and then discharge it. Every one of these has been raised, stamped and *closed* — closed by the same office that raised it, on the same day, with no work recorded in between.

That is not maintenance. That is a body of paper generated for the purpose of existing, and somebody has been generating it about this building, at a rate of two a year, for eleven years.
check.failure: Twenty-two forms, stamped, in a hand you have seen before. There is a convention they are violating and it stays just out of reach, filed somewhere behind everything else you have ever read.

clue.title: Raised and closed the same day
clue.text: Every repair notice in Hang-Hi was raised, stamped and closed by the same office on the same day, with no work recorded. Two a year for eleven years.

objects.name: the window over the harbour
objects.description:
The glass gives you the harbour, the fog, and the perpetual violet overhead going about its slow crimson business at an hour when a sky ought to have committed to something. Down there the water is holding whatever came out of it and is not offering it up, and the tide has been working at the same stretch of shingle for as long as you have been standing here.

And the sound is still there.

Rotors. Slow ones — the heavy, unhurried, entirely confident chop of a machine holding a position rather than travelling anywhere, somewhere off past the breakwater, in fog far too thick for any machine to be flying in.

It has not stopped since you came out of the water. Four days, at a constant bearing and a constant volume.

Nobody else has mentioned it. You have twice asked, in the specific casual voice a man uses when he wants an answer and does not want to be seen wanting one, and you have been answered both times in the specific casual voice a man uses when he has one ready — and the answer, both times, was about the weather.
objects.repeat: Still turning. Same position, same unhurried chop, same volume, same fog that could not possibly contain a machine that size and does anyway. Four days now. You have started timing it and it does not vary.

lucid.3: Listen to the rhythm rather than the sound. It is not rotors. It is a hand returning to the same four keys, over and over, while its owner works out what the next word is.

objects.monocle: The gold finds nothing over the water. No machine, no wreck, no oil, no debris field, no disturbance of any kind. The harbour is unmarked. The sound continues to arrive from a place where nothing is, at a volume that has never once varied, which is not how sound behaves and is exactly how a sound *effect* behaves.

passive.text: Constant volume, constant bearing, four days. A machine holding a hover for four days is a machine that is not a machine — fuel is not a matter of opinion, and neither is a gearbox. Whatever is over that harbour is not flying. It is simply *there*, making the noise of a thing that flies.

It is not that they cannot hear it. Watch a Reefer's face while the sound is happening: there is a small adjustment around the eyes, a half-beat of accommodation, and then nothing. They hear it. They have all agreed, without ever having had the conversation, to hear it as weather.

clue.title: Rotors over an empty harbour
clue.text: Four days of unvarying rotor noise from a fog bank containing nothing. Every Reefer asked has answered about the weather.

clue.title: No wreck
clue.text: Through the monocle the harbour is unmarked — no debris, no oil, no disturbance. Whatever you came down in did not come down in the water.

check.prompt: Open the window over the harbour and let the parish come in for a minute — the cold, the smell, the sound, and whatever else is riding on the sound at this hour.
check.success:
Cold off the water, green flame two streets down, and the rotors — and with the window open the rotors resolve into what they have been all along, which is not rotors.

It is a page being turned. Over and over, at the pace of a man checking something he has already read, from a room that is not in the direction the sound is coming from.
check.failure: Cold, and the smell of the harbour, and the rotors going on being rotors at the same unhurried pace they have kept since you came out of the water.

clue.title: Not rotors. Pages.
clue.text: With the window open the rotor sound resolves: a page being turned, over and over, from a room that is not where the sound is coming from.

objects.name: your desk
objects.description:
A door on two trestles, which is what a desk becomes when a man has decided that furniture is a distraction from the work being done on it.

Paper in drifts rather than stacks. A dozen abandoned openings to a dozen abandoned somethings, each one a single confident sentence followed by a very great deal of white — and the confidence is the part that stays with you, because a man who cannot start does not write like that. That is the handwriting of somebody who knows exactly how to begin and has stopped believing there is anywhere to go afterwards.

There is no typewriter on it.

There has never been a typewriter on it, in eleven years, and you would know, because it is your desk and you have sat at it every day.

There is, in the dust at the back edge where a hand does not go, a rectangle where the dust is thinner. Of a size. With four small round gaps at the corners.
objects.repeat: The rectangle in the dust has not filled in. Dust does not work like that — dust arrives on everything at the same rate, that is the entire nature of dust — and this rectangle has been holding its edges since before you started looking at it.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the rectangle is occupied. There is a typewriter there, black and heavy and mid-sentence, and it is not translucent or ghostly or any of the things the word would lead you to expect. It is simply present, and the room has been asked not to include it.

passive.text: Four round gaps at the corners of a thin rectangle. Feet — rubber ones, the kind fitted to office machines so they do not walk across a desk under their own vibration. That is not furniture. Furniture does not vibrate.

There is a cold cup somewhere under that paper and the ring beneath it is older than the cup is, which means there was a cup before this cup, in the same place, for long enough to leave its own mark. Somebody has sat here drinking the same thing at the same spot for years, and has not once moved the cup to wipe underneath it.

clue.title: The shape of an absent machine
clue.text: The dust on your desk holds a clean rectangle with four round gaps at the corners. Nothing has ever stood there. The dust disagrees.

check.prompt: The dust holds a rectangle with four round gaps at the corners and a worn arc on the near side. Work the machine out from its footprint, the way you would work out a man from his handwriting.
check.success:
Four feet, in a rectangle nine and a quarter by eleven and a half, with the front pair set inboard — which is a carriage-return frame, which means a heavy desk machine, which means a weight no man carries down a flight of stairs alone.

And the dust is undisturbed all round it. Nothing was dragged. Nothing was lifted. The rectangle is not where a machine was taken from. It is where a machine has not yet been put.
check.failure: A rectangle and four gaps and a quantity of dust, and it is the shape of a typewriter the way a hole is the shape of a thing that is not in it.

clue.title: Where it has not yet been put
clue.text: The dust around the absent machine on your desk is undisturbed on every side. Nothing was removed. The space is where something has not yet been placed.

objects.name: the seam in the hallway mirror
objects.description:
The mirror has stopped bothering.

It is not showing you the corridor and it is not showing you the office. It is showing you the *edge between them* — about four inches wide, with no thickness at all, the way the fold in a sheet of paper has no thickness — and the edge has been in this hallway the entire eleven years you have lived here, and has been visible for the last several days, and has not once been visible before that.

The office is on the other side of it. The lamp is on. The chair is pushed back from the desk and has been left pushed back. There is a page in the machine.

Nothing is stopping you. Nothing has been stopping you for some time now, and both of you know it.
objects.monocle: The gold makes no difference whatever. There is nothing left for it to reveal. That is the first time the monocle has had nothing to add, and it is the most alarming thing it has ever done.
objects.repeat: Still open. It is not going to close on its own, and that is not the same thing as it being patient, and you have caught yourself on three separate evenings standing in this corridor doing arithmetic about it.

passive.text: Every deduction you have made in a fortnight terminates here. There is nothing further to work out from this side, no reading of the evidence that does not require going and looking, and you have known that for at least a day and a half.

Four inches of nothing, and a floor on the other side that will take a man's weight — you can see the boards, you can see the grain in the boards. The body has already worked out the step. It is not the body that is hesitating.

check.prompt:
Go through. Nothing is stopping you and nothing has been stopping you for some time, and that is the part that will need thinking about afterwards, on the other side, if there is an afterwards and if there is a side.

There is no way back through a seam. Whatever is unfinished in Silvora Reefs stays unfinished.
check.success:
You go through.

There is no membrane and no cold and no drama, and the last thing behind you is somebody not saying anything, and then you are standing on boards in a room nine feet by eleven with a green-shaded lamp in it.
check.failure:
Your foot goes over the edge and your weight does not follow it, and you stand for a while in a doorway with one leg committed, which is not a dignified way to arrive anywhere and is a completely honest description of the last fortnight.

Then the knee that has been going since the harbour makes the decision for you, and you go through badly, and land on boards, in a room nine feet by eleven, with a green-shaded lamp in it.

objects.name: the clean rectangle on the floor
objects.description:
By the window, where the light would have been best for most of the day, the boards carry a rectangle about the size of a bread oven in which the dust is a different age from the dust around it.

Four small round depressions sit at its corners, pressed down into the grain over a period long enough that the wood has stopped intending to come back up. You can put a fingertip in one. It is deeper than a fingertip.

Whatever stood here stood here for years and it was heavy and it had feet rather than a base, and it was placed with some care — the rectangle is square to the window rather than square to the room, which is what a man does when what matters is the light falling on the work rather than the furniture looking tidy.

The boards around it are worn in a shallow arc on the near side. Somebody sat there. For a long time, in a chair that moved a little, doing something that required them to be close.
objects.repeat: The rectangle is where it was. The dust inside it is still the wrong age and is getting no older, and the four round depressions at the corners are still deeper than a fingertip, and the wear on the near side is still the shape of a man who sat there for years.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the rectangle is not empty. There is a machine in it, and it is being used, and the man using it has his back to you and does not turn round, and the light through the window falls on both of you at once from two different times of day.

passive.text: Four feet in a rectangle that size, at that spacing, bearing that much weight down into softwood over that many years: a platen machine. Something with a carriage that returns, which means something that takes a shock at the end of every line, which is why the feet are round and rubber and why they have driven themselves into the grain.

clue.title: Four round feet by the window
clue.text: A rectangle of differently-aged dust by the Hang-Hi window, with four round depressions pressed permanently into the grain. Something heavy stood there for years, in the best light in the room.

check.prompt: Something stood here for years and then did not. Reconstruct the removal.
check.success:
It went straight up.

A dragged object leaves a lip of dust at the trailing edge and a scar in the wax, and there is neither, on any of four sides. Somebody lifted a machine that takes two men, vertically, without tilting it, and did not scuff a board doing it.

And then the useful part, which is the dust inside the rectangle: it is *younger* than the dust outside. Not absent. Younger. Whatever this was has been taken away and put back and taken away again, repeatedly, over a long time — and the most recent time was inside the last fortnight, and it has not been put back yet.
check.failure: Dust ages by depth and by disturbance and by the light it has been sitting in, and this floor has had three different windows' worth of weather across it since anything stood here. The rectangle keeps its own counsel.

clue.title: Taken away and put back, repeatedly
clue.text: The machine that stood by the Hang-Hi window was lifted vertically, never dragged. The dust inside its footprint is younger than the dust around it: it has been removed and returned many times. The most recent removal was inside the last fortnight and it has not come back.

objects.name: the other tenants
objects.description:
Nine floors hanging off nothing at all, and on every one of them somebody is at home this evening.

There is a radio on four. It has been on since you came in and it is playing the sort of programme that is mostly talking, and it will go off at eleven, because it goes off at eleven. There is a bath running on six — the pipes announce it through the whole west stack, a long rising note that tops out and holds. And there is somebody on two who has been moving furniture for the better part of an hour and has not yet found where they want it.

It is a full building. It sounds exactly like a full building sounds on a cold evening: occupied, unremarkable, faintly companionable through a wall.

You have lived here eleven years.

You could not name one of them. Not one. Not a face on the stair, not a parcel taken in, not a nod at the letterboxes — and until this moment, standing in your own hallway listening to a bath you have heard a thousand times, it has never once struck you as strange.
objects.repeat: The radio on four is still on and has not changed station in eleven years. The bath on six ran at the usual hour and stopped at the usual hour. Nobody has come down the stairs all evening.
objects.monocle: Through the gold there is nobody on any of the floors. The radio is playing to an empty room, correctly, on schedule, and has been doing it for as long as the building has needed to sound occupied.

passive.text: The bath on six runs at the same hour every evening and stops at the same hour, and it runs for the same duration, and nobody has ever come down those stairs afterwards with wet hair. You have been in this stairwell at every hour of the day for eleven years.

clue.title: Eleven years, no neighbours
clue.text: Hang-Hi sounds fully occupied every evening — a radio, a bath, furniture moving. In eleven years of living here you have never met or named a single other tenant.

check.prompt: Nine floors of people you have never met, all of them at home, all of them audible. Reach for the building the way you would reach for the parish and see what comes back.
check.success:
Nothing comes back.

Not silence — the parish is loud tonight and it is entirely available from here, the queue moving at Mary's and the fire settling at Ben's and Luigi three floors down doing the west end first. All of that arrives, at full strength, from streets away.

From inside this building, at a range of forty feet, through two floors: nothing at all. There is a radio on four and a bath running on six and there is nobody behind either of them, and the parish does not extend into Hang-Hi, and Asimov's office is the last room in the building that has anybody in it.
check.failure: A radio, a bath, and somebody shifting a wardrobe about on two. It is an occupied building on an ordinary evening and it declines, courteously, to be anything else.

clue.title: The parish does not extend into this building
clue.text: Reaching for Hang-Hi the way you would reach for the parish returns nothing — while the rest of the town arrives at full strength from streets away. The radio and the bath have nobody behind them. Asimov's office is the last occupied room.

exits.durry_kwain: down the hill, past the green lamps, to the only counter in town that has ever been glad to see you
exits.mobius: along the harbour road to a building that gets you back where you started without ever asking you to turn
exits.rest_assured: up, into the obsidian, where the town keeps the ones who have finished
exits.dudes_dews: four minutes downhill to the busiest counter in the parish
exits.gs_spot: a walk nobody has ever been able to give you directions for
